headline: Bunker Pushing North Toward the Hook — Blues Right Behind Them, Fluke Holding the Channels
subhead: Bait pods moving up from Belmar are about to test the Hook rip, and the fluke bite is buying time while we wait.
body_markdown:
I made my call Tuesday morning standing on the Perth Amboy waterfront watching gulls work a nervous patch of water off the ferry terminal, and it wasn't close: I'm staging at the mouth of the bay this week, not deep in the back rivers. Bunker schools have been grinding north along the Jersey beach out of the Belmar stretch for a week now, and when that bait rounds Sandy Hook and pushes into the Reach, everything with teeth follows it in. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said it would spread up the coast as long as the weather stayed calm — and here it is, knocking on our door. I don't want to be sitting in the Navesink chasing weakfish scraps when that show finally walks into Raritan Bay.

So here's the split I'm working. Mornings and evenings, I'm running the Hook rip and the ferry channel edge off Highlands, watching for surface commotion on the tide change. That's historically the first place this pattern shows itself locally — bunker get squeezed against the rip current and the blues pile on top in broad daylight, which is unusual for this time of year but exactly what's happening south of us right now off Belmar and LBI. If you see diving birds and nervous water anywhere between the Hook and Romer Shoal, don't wait — cast straight into it. Poppers and 2-ounce metal, Ava jigs in white or bunker-flake pattern, whatever you can get out there fast. These blues aren't picky when they're on top of bait, but they will move on you quick, so keep the boat mobile and don't burn ten minutes on a spot that's gone quiet.

Striped bass are trickier right now, and I want to be straight about that. With water this warm — the ocean side is reading mid-70s, and the bay follows right behind it — the bigger keeper-class bass have gone nocturnal on us, same as everywhere south of the Cape. Daytime bites inside the bay have been soft. My best action has come after dark and right around first light, working bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs at Romer Shoal and along the edge of Flynn's Knoll in 15 to 20 feet, incoming tide preferred so the current stacks bait against the structure. If you can get out with live bunker on a slider rig, snag one out of a pod near the rip and drop it back — that's produced my two best fish of the month, both mid-20s, neither one during daylight hours. Don't expect a blitz-style bass bite to show up behind the bunker the way the blues have; right now the stripers are playing it cautious and low-light, and that's likely to hold until we get a stretch of cooler nights.

Fluke have been the honest workhorse of the bay all month, and they're not asking us to wait for anything. The channel edges through the Reach and along Keyport Flats have been steady — not a banner bite, but a dependable one, which is more than I can say for the bass right now. I've been dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails along the drop-offs where the flats spill into the channel, 18 to 25 feet, working the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping your line sideways. Chartreuse tipped with a strip of squid has been the better combo on the duller days, and I'm seeing keeper fish mixed in with plenty of shorts — nothing like that 12-plus-pound doormat that got weighed in last month, but solid 18-to-20 inch fish if you cover ground and stay on the bottom. Romer Shoal has held fish too, though boat traffic there gets thick on weekends, so I'd fish it early or middle of the week if you can.

Weakfish and porgies are around in the usual spots — Navesink holds a few weakfish if you're working bloodworms or small soft plastics on the bottom near the drop-offs after dark, and porgies are scattered on the structure around Romer Shoal for anyone bottom fishing with clam — but neither is worth building a trip around right now. They're a bonus, not a plan.

Looking at the week ahead, the moon's sliding into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which means softer current and wider fishing windows rather than short, violent tide changes. That's actually good news for the bunker push — less current to scatter the pods as they work north, which should keep them concentrated and visible as they round the Hook. If the weather holds calm like it has, I expect the blue blitz to show itself inside the bay within the next couple days, probably first at the Hook rip or the ferry channel on a tide change. My plan is simple: fluke in the middle of the day when nothing's popping on top, bunker chunks and live bait after dark for the bass, and rods rigged and ready for metal the second birds start working. If the bunker slide past us instead of stacking up, I'll pivot back to the channel program full time — the fluke aren't going anywhere.
